 1 Introduction These are the reasons for decision in the claim to be a Convention refugee made by XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. Ms. XXXXX is a 40-year-old mother of two children who live in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia with their father who is the claimant's husband. The claim is against Ethiopia and the ground is nationality. Ms. XXXXX is Eritrean through her mother's family. Allegations The claimant said that when she left Ethiopia in XXXX, 1998, it was not her intention to claim refugee status. She travelled on a valid Ethiopian passport stamped with a valid Canadian visitor's visa. She said the purpose of her trip to Canada was to attend her nephew's wedding. She said it was also her intention to visit relatives in the United States. She said she never made the trip to the U.S. but met several of the relatives at the wedding in Ottawa. While in Canada the claimant applied for and obtained an extension of her visitor visa under the pretext that she wanted to attend another wedding. She claimed Convention refugee status 16 June 1999, though she said she had already made plans to return to Ethiopia XX XXXX 1999. She said her reason for changing her mind about returning home was the break out of the current war between Ethiopia and Eritrea in May 1998, and the subsequent mass deportations to Eritrea given women and children of full or part Eritrean origin that occurred quickly the following month after hostilities began. She said that most deportees had been born in Ethiopia or had worked there as citizens prior to Eritrea achieving independence from Ethiopia in 1991. The claimant said that she ha d always considered herself an Ethiopian, though her sister, who had died under highly questionable circumstances, was an activist in the Eritrean cause. She said her mother is missing and nothing is known as to what happened to her. She said both her sister and mother voted in the Er itrean referendum of 1993. The claimant also said that her sister's husband was among those who were rounded up and deported to Eritrea by the Ethiopian authorities in March, 1999. In addition, she said that her husband in Addis Ababa was detained for 17 days by the Ethiopian authorities. Analysis The panel is concerned about two issues in this claim: the claimant's credibility and the chances of her being identified as an Eritrean for deportation purposes on her return. The panel accepts counsel's argument on credibility contained in his submissions at the bottom of page 4 of that document.

 2 "… She is the mother of two very young children whom she has not seen for almost two years. If her original inten tion was to claim refugee status why would she have waited so long? After all, the war had already begun when she left Ethiopia in 1998. Why did she seek an extension of her visitor status instead of claiming refugee status? She has a sister and a nephew in Canada and she had already spent several months in the country. It is common knowledge that, unlike refugee claimants, visitors are not entitled to any social assistance. It is respectfully submitted that when evaluated in this context, Ms. XXXXX's conduct and actions are consistent with those of a person who was constrained by circumstances beyond her control to resort to courses of action she would not otherwise have undertaken. In this regard, there is no doubt that the situation in Ethiopia continued to deteriorate from the time of her departure." In addition to the above, the panel finds that the claimant was credible in both her testimony concerning her story and on the evidence she submitted in her file. On the second issue, her being identified as an Eritrean and running a high risk of being deported to Eritrea, the panel finds that based on the credible facts, there is more than a mere possibility that the claimant would be identified as an Eritrean and at risk of persecution based on the documentary evidence, and her testimony with respect to what has already happened to her sister and brother-in-law, and her mother. The panel finds that even though the claimant has always considered herself to be Ethiopian and ne ver took part in Eritrean politics, it would not be difficult for Ethiopian officials to link her to her mother and sister, and her marriage to an Ethiopian would not persuade officials that she should remain in Ethiopia, nor would her family be able to join her. The documentary evidence, Exhibit R-1, Tab 1 at page 2, states "the government continued to detain and deport w ithout due process Eritreans and Ethiopians of Eritrean origin. Since the outbreak of border conflict in May, 1998, more than 67,000 such persons have left Ethiopia for Eritrea; a vast majority were deported, although a small number left voluntarily. Tab 1 at page 15 of the same document indicates that identification of ethnic- origin can occur as a result of the referendum", (of 1993). The claimant said that both her mother and sister had voted in that referendum and from this the Ethiopian authorities would find out that she was an Eritrean. In August, 1999, the government decreed that all Eritreans 18 yeas of age and above residing in Ethiopia who either had taken part in the 1993 referendum or the independence of Eritea from Ethiopia, or who had been granted Eritrean citizenship, had to register as aliens immediately. Those registeri ng would be issued an identity card and given a six month residence permit; however, this permit does not permit individuals access to hospitals or other public services. The document also states that the Ethiopian passports of residents of Eritrean origin routinely were confiscated or restricted in use for a single exit and no re-entry. The panel finds on a balance of probabilities that the claimant would experience this fate were she to return to Addis Ababa.

 3 Determination The panel finds that there would be more than a mere possibility that the claimant would be identified as an Eritrean were she to return to Ethiopia and the fate visited upon thousands of other Eritreans mentioned above would befall her as well. Decision The panel finds that XXXXXXXX XXXXXX XXXXX is a Convention refugee as defined in Section 2(1) of the Immigration Act. “XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX” XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Dated at Ottawa, the 27th day of April, 2000.
